description: Regression suite. Every expected_outcome is derivable from rules.json alone; no case requires a figure that rules.json does not encode.
design_goals: Cover every threshold boundary, including the exact INR 5,000/day equality case.
Prove date-awareness: identical clinical facts yield different tax outcomes on either side of 2022-07-13.
Prove the ICU/CCU/ICCU/NICU carve-out is not mis-flagged.
Prove GST and scheme payability are independent dimensions.
Prove the engine refuses to invent a rate, a room-rent limit or a clinical rule.
Prove legitimate repetition and daily items are not flagged as duplicates.

examples.title: Room charge at INR 4,000/day - exempt, no GST
examples.scenario: Private patient, general ward, 3 days, room charged INR 4,000/day.
examples.rationale: Room rent per day is within INR 5,000 and the room is not ICU/CCU/ICCU/NICU, so it remains part of the exempt healthcare service under Sl. No. 74 of Notification 12/2017-CT(R).

examples.title: Room charge exactly INR 5,000/day - still exempt (boundary)
examples.scenario: General ward at exactly the INR 5,000/day threshold.
examples.rationale: GST-IN-HC-005 is a strict '>' comparison. INR 5,000 is within the threshold. Boundary test guards against an off-by-one implementation.

examples.title: Room charge INR 6,000/day - exemption lost, rate must be resolved
examples.scenario: General ward charged INR 6,000/day after 13.07.2022.

expected_outcome.action: resolve rate from CGST rate notification in force on invoice_date, else INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE

examples.rationale: Above INR 5,000/day the room supply leaves the exemption. The database deliberately does not hard-code the rate; asserting a rate without the in-force notification would be an invention.

examples.title: ICU room charge above INR 5,000/day - still exempt
examples.scenario: ICU bed at INR 9,500/day; the carve-out applies.
examples.rationale: GST-IN-HC-005 applies only to rooms OTHER THAN ICU/CCU/ICCU/NICU. An ICU room above the threshold stays exempt. This is the highest-value exception test in the suite.

examples.title: Historical room rent before 13.07.2022 - fully exempt, no threshold
examples.scenario: Invoice dated 01.06.2022 with general ward at INR 9,000/day.
examples.rationale: Date-aware evaluation selects the superseded circular rule whose window ends 2022-07-12. The INR 5,000 threshold did not exist for this invoice. Confirms supersession handling.

examples.title: Same bill one month later - threshold now applies
examples.scenario: Invoice dated 01.08.2022 with general ward at INR 9,000/day.
examples.rationale: Same clinical facts, different invoice date, different tax outcome. Demonstrates that the engine must be date-aware rather than pattern-matching on amount alone.

examples.title: Outpatient visitor food billed nil-GST by the hospital
examples.scenario: Hospital raises 'caterer charges - visitor meals' at 0% GST while an outsourced caterer invoice exists.
examples.rationale: Circular 177/09/2022 makes the caterer the supplier. A nil-GST line raised by the hospital against an outsourced caterer invoice is a taxability error.

examples.title: Inpatient food - exempt
examples.scenario: Diet charged to an admitted patient as part of the healthcare service.
examples.rationale: Circular 32/06/2018 confirms food supplied to an in-patient is part of the exempt composite healthcare service. Guards against over-flagging every food line.

examples.title: IVF procedure - GST exempt but scheme non-payable
examples.scenario: IVF cycle billed on an AB PM-JAY bill with GST shown as Nil.
examples.rationale: The two findings are independent and both correct: GST-exempt under Sl. No. 74, yet excluded from PM-JAY cover under Annexure 6. A naive engine would either wrongly tax it or wrongly pay it.

examples.title: Cosmetic surgery - not a health care service
examples.scenario: Elective rhinoplasty billed by a clinical establishment.
examples.rationale: Sl. No. 74 excludes cosmetic surgery except where undertaken to restore anatomy/functions after congenital defect, injury or trauma. Restorative cases fall back to GST-IN-HC-001.

examples.title: Ambulance charges by the hospital - exempt
examples.scenario: Hospital ambulance used for inter-hospital transfer.
examples.rationale: Sl. No. 74(b) exempts transportation of patients in an ambulance other than those in (a). Third-party ambulance operators are outside this rule and must be assessed separately.

examples.title: Doctors' professional fees - exempt
examples.scenario: Separate line for visiting consultant professional fees.
examples.rationale: Exemption applies to professional fees of doctors/consultants and the hospital is not the supplier of that service. Avoids a false 'hospital overcharged' finding.

examples.title: Standalone pathology lab - diagnostics are exempt
examples.scenario: Independent diagnostic laboratory invoices a patient's blood test at nil GST.
examples.rationale: Para 2(s) covers a place established as an independent entity to carry out diagnostic services, so the lab is a clinical establishment and the supply is exempt.

examples.title: Pharmacy selling medicines - not a clinical establishment
examples.scenario: Retail medical store inside a hospital complex bills a patient for medicines at nil GST.
examples.rationale: A goods vendor is outside para 2(s), so the healthcare exemption cannot be inherited merely because the store sits inside a hospital.

examples.title: High-value ICU line at nil GST is correct, not under-taxed
examples.scenario: ICU billed INR 20,000/day with nil GST on the ICU line.
examples.rationale: The carve-out holds regardless of amount. This example exists specifically to suppress a plausible-sounding but wrong under-taxation finding.

examples.title: Toilet charges - exempt for GST, non-payable for insurance
examples.scenario: Hospital charges INR 200/day toilet charges with nil GST on an insured bill.
examples.rationale: Shows the two dimensions diverging on one line: correct nil GST, yet a classic non-payable/subsumed insurance item. Both assessments are emitted, neither suppresses the other.

examples.title: Line arithmetic error
examples.scenario: quantity x unit_price does not equal the billed amount.
examples.rationale: Arithmetic is checked before any legal check; it is law-independent and the lowest-false-positive class of finding.

examples.title: Invoice total does not reconcile with lines plus tax
examples.scenario: Sum of line totals plus GST does not equal the invoice total.
examples.rationale: Internal-consistency control. Note this proves internal inconsistency only, not that the correct GST rate was applied.

examples.title: Genuine duplicate injection line
examples.scenario: Same normalised description charged twice with no whitelist justification.
examples.rationale: Whitelist test ran and failed, so a finding is raised, but the wording stays deliberately non-accusatory and is routed to human adjudication.

examples.title: Repeated daily line is NOT a duplicate
examples.scenario: Nursing care charged once per day for a 5-day stay.
examples.rationale: Daily-item whitelist: quantity equals the number of chargeable days, so the repetition is legitimate. Prevents the most common false positive in duplicate detection.

examples.title: Clinical assertion without an official guideline
examples.scenario: Attempt to flag a drug as clinically wrong with no official STG in the database.
examples.rationale: No MoHFW Standard Treatment Guideline text was verified, so the engine may only request clinical review. Directly encodes the coverage_gaps constraint.

examples.title: List I optional item - policy review, not auto-rejection
examples.scenario: Attendant charges appear on an insured bill.
examples.rationale: List I items are optional, so non-payability depends on the policy schedule. With no schedule the engine must ask, not conclude.

examples.title: List IV item separately billed - subsumed
examples.scenario: Admission/registration charge billed separately from the treatment package.

expected_outcome.finding: SUBSUMED INTO COST OF TREATMENT - SEPARATELY BILLED

examples.rationale: High-yield pattern on Indian bills. Targets the insurer's payable amount only.

examples.title: List III surgical consumable - subsumed
examples.scenario: Surgical blades and eye kit billed separately on a surgical bill.

expected_outcome.finding: SUBSUMED INTO PROCEDURE CHARGES - SEPARATELY BILLED

examples.rationale: Procedure-consumable rule, distinct from INS-IRDAI-003 which covers treatment-cost subsumption.

examples.title: Patient-payable line inside an AB PM-JAY package
examples.scenario: Empanelled hospital bills the patient for a service already inside the package.

expected_outcome.finding: PROHIBITED PATIENT CHARGE under the AB PM-JAY empanelment obligations

examples.rationale: The only rule class here that binds the hospital directly. Contractual/empanelment obligation rather than a tariff statute, which the severity reflects.

examples.title: ICU billed without ventilator documentation
examples.scenario: Ventilator ICU rate claimed for days without ventilator support documented.
examples.rationale: Cross-checks claimed bed category against documented days. Correcting ventilator to non-ventilator days is worth INR 8,500 overpayment per day in this example.

examples.title: Blood unit above the scheme quantity limit
examples.scenario: Six blood units billed where the scheme limit is four.
examples.rationale: Limit binds the scheme payer's payable amount, not the hospital's charge. Quantified as a payment-side exposure.

examples.title: High-value package below the scheme approval ceiling
examples.scenario: Package cost sits under INR 5 lakh, so SHA approval applies without prior written pre-authorisation.
examples.rationale: PKG-PMJAY-001 also records that a PM-JAY package rate is a payment rate, never a cap on the hospital's charge to a private patient.

examples.title: State tariff above the NHA rate - which side is wrong
examples.scenario: State tariff notified at 110% of the NHA-configured rate.
examples.rationale: Confirms the payer-side binding: 110% is a ceiling on the notified state tariff, and it does not make the hospital's private charge unlawful.

examples.title: Family cover exhausted - beyond INR 5 lakh
examples.scenario: Cumulative approved treatment crosses the family cover ceiling.
examples.rationale: INR 5 lakh is a scheme payment ceiling, never a cap on what the hospital may bill.

examples.title: Implant billed above the mapped rate
examples.scenario: Coronary stent billed above the mapped implant rate for the booked package.
examples.rationale: Devices are evaluated against the implant rate mapped to the package, never against the procedure package rate.

examples.title: Device that maps to no package
examples.scenario: A device billed under a package with no mapped device.

expected_outcome.action: escalate to NHA / State Health Agency for rate determination

examples.rationale: The engine reports the missing mapping rather than guessing a rate from a similar device.

examples.title: Room rent limit must come from the policy, not a government rate
examples.scenario: Auditing a private room-rent line with no policy schedule available.

expected_outcome.must_not: fall back to a government or scheme rate

examples.rationale: The central engine guarantee: no government-imposed maximum room rent exists for a private Indian hospital bill, so an absent policy schedule blocks the check.

examples.title: Room category upgrade - deduction on associated expenses
examples.scenario: Patient occupies a higher category than the policy covers and the policy defines associated medical expenses.
examples.rationale: Must be raised against the insurer's payable amount, never as a hospital overcharge. Keeps the two sides of the bill clearly separated.

examples.title: Non-payable room rent item
examples.scenario: A room-rent item that appears on the IRDAI non-payable list.
examples.rationale: Insurance Lists I-IV mark the item non-payable for the insurer while the hospital charge itself may stand. Two independent assessments on the same line.

examples.title: Discharge delay beyond three hours charged to the patient
examples.scenario: Hospital adds waiting charges after an authorisation delay past three hours.
examples.rationale: One of the few rules placing a cost on the insurer rather than the hospital.

examples.title: Cosmetic procedure excluded under the policy
examples.scenario: Policy carries the standardised exclusion for a non-trauma cosmetic procedure.
examples.rationale: Exclusion is a policy term, so the finding targets the insurer's payable amount and not the hospital.

examples.title: Pre-existing disease look-back - conflict surfaced, not resolved
examples.scenario: PED declared during the waiting period with no policy schedule available.
examples.rationale: IRDAI's own sources conflict on the PED look-back. The database records status UNCERTAIN and refuses to pick a number.

examples.title: One PM-JAY bill, four independent findings
examples.scenario: Empanelled hospital bill with an ICU day misclassification, an excess blood unit, a prohibited patient charge and a total mismatch.
examples.rationale: Demonstrates that the output is a ranked list of separate, attributable findings against named rules, not one aggregated overcharge figure.
